parts.instructions: Read what each person is looking for. Match each person to the best text. There are three extra texts.

people.text: Ahmet is interested in history. He would like to find out how people lived in the desert hundreds of years ago and see the objects they used.
Adriana wants to sleep outside and look at the stars, far away from the lights of any town.
Abdul loves traditional food. He would like to taste bread that is baked in a hole in the sand.
Afia is travelling with two small children. She wants a short, easy activity in the early morning, before it gets too hot.

texts.title: Dune Buggy Races
texts.text: Drive a fast buggy up and down the biggest sand hills. You must be at least sixteen years old.

texts.title: The Cactus House
texts.text: A glass garden with plants from dry countries. A guide explains how each one stores water in its leaves and stem.

texts.title: Starlight Camp
texts.text: Spend the night in a tent in the middle of the desert. There are no lights for fifty kilometres, so the sky is perfect.

texts.title: Desert Restaurant
texts.text: Eat lamb and rice at a long table in a tent. The bread is bought from a shop in town; nothing is baked in the sand.

texts.title: Museum of Desert Life
texts.text: See tools, clothes and houses from the past, and learn how families crossed the sand in the days before cars.

texts.title: Family Camel Walk
texts.text: A gentle walk at sunrise with a camel guide. It lasts thirty minutes and is made for parents with young children.

texts.title: Oasis Lodge
texts.text: A hotel in the middle of the desert with cool rooms and a pool. The lights stay on all night.

texts.title: Village Bread Day
texts.text: Join the families of a small village to make flat bread and bake it in the hot sand. You can eat it fresh with honey.

parts.title: A week with my uncle in Morocco
parts.instructions: Read the article and choose the best answer for each question.
parts.passage:
Last summer, I stayed for a week with my uncle Karim, who lives in a small town on the edge of the Sahara. I was very excited, because I had only seen the desert in films.

On the first morning, my uncle woke me at five. "We must walk before the sun gets high," he said. It was already warm, but the sand was cool under my feet. We climbed a big dune, and from the top I could see nothing but gold in every direction. I felt very small.

My uncle works as a guide, and he taught me a lot. He showed me how to wrap a long scarf around my head to keep out the sun and the sand. He also told me never to go anywhere without at least two litres of water, even for a short walk.

The nights were the best part. After dinner, we lay on a blanket and counted the shooting stars. I had never seen so many. When I left, my uncle gave me a small bag of sand from the dune. It is on my desk now, and every time I look at it, I want to go back.

questions.prompt: Why was the writer excited about the visit?
options: He wanted to learn to speak Arabic
He had never stayed with his uncle
He had only seen deserts in films
His uncle had promised him a camel ride
questions.explanation: He had only seen the desert in films.

questions.prompt: Why did they walk early in the morning?
options: They wanted to see the stars
The sun was not high yet
His uncle had to go to work
The sand was too cold later
questions.explanation: They must walk before the sun gets high.

questions.prompt: How did the writer feel on top of the dune?
options: Very small in the big landscape
questions.explanation: From the top he could see gold in every direction and felt very small.

questions.prompt: What rule did his uncle give him about water?
options: Take at least two litres with you
Never walk further than a kilometre
Leave some in a bottle at home
Drink only when you feel thirsty
questions.explanation: He told him never to go anywhere without at least two litres of water.

questions.prompt: What did the writer do in the evenings?
options: He studied maps with his uncle
He helped to cook dinner for guests
He watched shooting stars at night
He wrote letters to his friends
questions.explanation: After dinner they lay on a blanket and counted shooting stars.

parts.title: The camel, the ship of the desert
parts.instructions: Choose the sentence that fits each gap. There are three extra sentences.
parts.passage:
People often call the camel the ship of the desert, and there is a good reason for this. [1] It can walk for many days across hot sand and carry a heavy load.

A camel has a hump on its back. Many people think the hump is full of water, but this is not true. [2] When there is no food, the camel slowly uses the fat, and the hump gets smaller.

Camels also have very long eyelashes. [3] Their wide, flat feet help them too, because they do not sink into the soft sand.

Although camels can live without water for a long time, they drink a lot when they find it. [4] After that, they can walk again for a week or more.

For thousands of years, people have used camels for travel and trade. [5] Today, they are still important in many places, and some tourists enjoy riding them.
sentences: Camels were first brought to Australia about two hundred years ago.
Without them, long journeys across the desert would have been almost impossible.
It stores fat, which gives the animal energy when it is hungry.
They protect the eyes from the wind and the blowing sand.
The animal is perfectly made for a life in very dry places.
A thirsty camel can drink over a hundred litres in only a few minutes.
Their milk is drunk in many parts of the desert.
A baby camel can stand up and walk a few hours after it is born.

gaps.explanation: The sentence about being perfectly made for dry places follows the name "ship of the desert" and leads to "it can walk for many days".
The hump is not full of water, but it stores fat, which the next sentence says the camel uses.
The eyelashes protect the eyes from the wind and sand, and the next sentence adds the feet.
The camel drinks a hundred litres in minutes, and "after that" it can walk for a week.
Journeys across the desert would have been almost impossible without them, which links to "used camels for travel".

parts.title: A postcard from Dubai
parts.instructions: Choose the correct word for each gap.
parts.passage: Dear Hannah, We have been in Dubai for three days and it is incredibly hot! The temperature [1] up to forty degrees every afternoon, so we stay inside until five o'clock. Yesterday, we [2] to the top of the tallest building in the world. The view was amazing, [3] I was a little afraid of the height. Tomorrow we are going on a desert safari, and I have never [4] on a camel before. I am sure that I will [5] some great photos. I miss you, and I [6] you a present from the market yesterday. See you soon! Dina

questions.explanation: "Gets" or "reaches" describes the temperature rising to forty degrees; the others do not fit the pattern.

questions.prompt: Gap 3
questions.explanation: The view was amazing, but she was afraid: contrast.

questions.prompt: Gap 4
questions.explanation: Have never + past participle.

questions.prompt: Gap 5
questions.explanation: Take photos is the usual collocation.

questions.prompt: Gap 6
questions.explanation: Dina has already bought the present at the market, so the past simple is correct.

parts.title: Staying cool in hot weather
parts.instructions: Write one word in each gap.
parts.passage: When the weather is very hot, it is important to look after yourself. First of all, you should drink plenty of water, even [1] you do not feel thirsty. It is also a good idea to wear light clothes and a hat to keep the sun [2] your head. Many people go out early in the morning or late in the evening, when it is much [3] hot. During the middle of the day, it is better to stay [4] a cool room or in the shade. Children and old people need extra care, because they can get ill [5] quickly. If you feel dizzy, sit down and rest [6] a few minutes.

gaps.explanation: "Even if you do not feel thirsty" is a fixed phrase.
Keep the sun off your head.
Much less hot: comparison of a smaller degree.
They can get ill more quickly.

parts.title: Short conversations
parts.instructions: Listen to seven short conversations. Choose the correct answer.

turns.speaker: m
turns.text: So, Adriana, when shall we walk to the oasis? I’d like to see the palm trees.

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: The guide said we should go before lunch, but I think it’s already too hot at that time. We were going to leave at eleven, and it would be forty degrees.

turns.speaker: m
turns.text: What about the afternoon, then, when the shade is short?

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: That’s the hottest time of all. People get ill. I’d rather wait for the evening, once the sun has set. It’s cooler, and the sky will be full of stars.

turns.speaker: m
turns.text: Good idea. I’ll tell the guide and bring a torch.

question.prompt: When will they walk to the oasis?
question.explanation: The morning plan is too hot and the afternoon is the hottest time; they will walk in the evening after the sun has set.

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: Aiko, how much water should I take on the hike tomorrow? Two bottles?

turns.speaker: m
turns.text: Two is not enough. Last time I took two bottles and I finished them by noon, and I was thirsty all afternoon. My guide always carries four, but that’s because he walks the whole day, all the way to the next village. For a half day like yours, I’d say three. It’s heavy but you’ll be glad.

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: Okay, three it is. Where can I buy them?

turns.speaker: m
turns.text: At the shop next to the hotel. They’re cheap.

question.prompt: How many bottles does the man suggest?
question.explanation: Two bottles were not enough for him and four is for a whole day; for her half day he suggests three.

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: Hi, Ahmet, it’s Afia. I’m at the desert camp and I wanted to say sorry for forgetting to take the photos you wanted. And I’m sorry too that I was late. I packed in a hurry. I nearly forgot my sun cream, but I found it at the last moment, and I have a big bottle of water in my bag, so I’m safe. What I did leave at home are my sunglasses, and the light here is so strong that my eyes hurt. I’ll buy some in the market tomorrow. Speak soon.

question.explanation: She nearly forgot the sun cream but found it, and she has a bottle of water; she left her sunglasses at home.

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: Aarav, why are you wearing that long white shirt in this heat? Most tourists wear shorts.

turns.speaker: m
turns.text: People often think it’s for photos, and I do look quite smart in it, but that’s not the point. The sleeves protect me from the sun, and the white colour reflects the light. The air can move under it, so it feels much cooler than a T-shirt.

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: What about mosquitoes? I thought it was to keep insects away.

turns.speaker: m
turns.text: There are hardly any here at this time of year. It’s really the temperature.

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: Now I understand. I’ll buy one too.

question.prompt: Why does the man wear a long white shirt?
question.explanation: He says the photos and the insects are not the reason; the white shirt reflects the light and lets air through, so he is cooler.

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: Attention, please. This is an announcement for passengers on the desert railway. The timetable on the wall says that the train to the coast leaves at nine, but that is the old timetable. Last week, the leaving time was changed to eleven, and some of you may have read that on the website. However, we have just received news of a change. The train will leave at ten o’clock today because of the heat. Please come to platform two by a quarter to ten. Thank you for your patience, and have a nice journey.

question.prompt: What time does the train leave now?
question.explanation: The wall says nine and the website says eleven, but the train leaves at ten today because of the heat.

turns.speaker: m
turns.text: Hi, Adriana, it’s Adebayo. I did the camel ride yesterday, as I told you I would. I wasn’t frightened at the start, even though the camel stood up so suddenly, and I thought the ride would be longer, but after an hour it felt quite enough. The problem came afterwards. When I got down, my legs hurt, my back hurt, everything hurt. I could hardly walk to the hotel, and I’m still stiff today. I’m glad that I tried it, but I won’t do it again soon. Call me.

question.prompt: How does the man feel about the ride?
options: The ride was far too short
question.explanation: He was not frightened and the ride was long enough, but afterwards he was stiff and in pain.

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: It’s so hot, Achille! Shall we get an ice cream? There’s a van over there.

turns.speaker: m
turns.text: Good idea. I’m going to have a cone. Or maybe a fruit salad, they look healthy.

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: I’d love an ice cream, but it will melt in a minute, and my hands will be sticky. And the fruit salad takes ages. What I really want is something cold to drink, with lots of ice.

turns.speaker: m
turns.text: Orange juice?

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: Perfect, I’ll have that. A large one, please.

question.explanation: She likes the idea of ice cream but it would melt, and the fruit salad is slow; she wants a cold drink with ice.

parts.title: Understanding the main idea
parts.instructions: Listen to six short conversations and choose the best answer.

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: I saw the camel trek in the brochure, Ahmet. Did you book it?

turns.speaker: m
turns.text: Yes, I did. People told me it was a lot of money, and I was a bit worried at first, because it’s more than the hotel for a night.

turns.speaker: f

turns.speaker: m
turns.text: Look at the sky, Agnieszka. It’s turning orange. I think a sandstorm is coming.

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: Shall we stay in the tent until it’s over? We have food and water.

turns.speaker: m
turns.text: The tent won’t hold in strong wind, and I read that these storms can last a day. The guide has gone to town, so we can’t ask him.

turns.speaker: f

turns.speaker: m

turns.speaker: f

question.explanation: The tent is not safe and the guide has gone, so they decide to leave now by car for the village.

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: Aiden, I have good news. My photo of the dunes won the prize at the competition!

turns.speaker: m
turns.text: That’s fantastic! I knew you would. You worked so hard on it.

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: Thank you. I thought you might feel a bit jealous, because you entered too.

turns.speaker: m
turns.text: Honestly, no. I’m just happy. My picture was nothing special. And the trip to get yours wasn’t cheap, so now it was worth it.

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: You always say kind things.

turns.speaker: m
turns.text: It’s true. When are you going to show it to everybody?

question.prompt: How does Aiden feel about Abimbola's news?
question.explanation: Aiden says he is not jealous and the cost was worth it; he says he knew she would win, so he is proud of her.

turns.speaker: m
turns.text: I’m going to sleep in the desert tomorrow, Aiko. I’ll only bring light clothes.

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: That’s what I did the first time, and I was freezing. The days are hot, but at night it falls to almost zero.

turns.speaker: m
turns.text: Really? I thought I should buy a hat in the market.

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: You’ll need one for the day, of course, and walking early helps. But take a thick coat. You’ll be glad of it when the sun goes down.

turns.speaker: m
turns.text: Thanks for the warning. I’ll borrow my brother’s.

question.prompt: What does Aiko advise Adebayo to do?
options: Wear a hat in the market
Take a warm coat for the night
question.explanation: She says the days are hot but the night is cold; a hat and an early start are good, but the main advice is the warm coat.

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: Which hotel shall we choose, Abdul? The big one by the pool, or the small one in the old town?

turns.speaker: m
turns.text: The small one. I know the pool looks nice, but there’s a party every night, and the music goes on till two.

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: The price is almost the same, isn’t it? And I heard the food at the big hotel is better.

turns.speaker: m
turns.text: I’m sure it is, and I don’t mind eating in town. What I want is a good night’s sleep. In the old town it’s silent after ten.

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: Okay, you’ve convinced me.

question.prompt: Why does Abdul prefer the small hotel?
question.explanation: They say the prices are similar and the food is better at the big hotel, but he picks the small one for the quiet at night.

turns.speaker: m
turns.text: Are you ready for the museum, Afia?

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: I’d love to go, honestly. I’ve wanted to see it for years. But it’s closed on Mondays, and today’s Monday. I didn’t read the sign.

turns.speaker: m
turns.text: Never mind, we can see the old fort instead.

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: I’ve seen enough forts. I’m so disappointed, because tomorrow we fly home early. This was my only chance.

turns.speaker: m
turns.text: What a shame. Maybe next time?

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: I hope so. I’ll put it on my list.

question.prompt: How does Afia feel about the museum?
question.explanation: She has wanted to go for years, but it is closed and she flies home tomorrow, so she is sorry she cannot go.

parts.title: A talk about the Sahara
parts.instructions: Listen to the talk and complete each note. Write one or two words, a number, a date or a time.

turns.speaker: saskia
turns.text: Good afternoon, everybody. Today, I will tell you about the Sahara, the largest hot desert in the world. It is about as big as the United States. Some books say that it covers nine countries, but that is not the whole picture. Most experts count eleven countries, from Egypt in the east to Morocco in the west. Many people think the Sahara is just sand, like in the films. But only about a fifth of the desert is sand. Another part is rocky, with mountains, and a large part is flat and stony, like a plain. The sand dunes are famous, but they are not the biggest part. Now, the weather. Here we have some surprises. During the day it can reach fifty degrees in summer. Last July, it was forty-eight in one place, which was a record at that time. But at night, it can fall to zero, so people need warm clothes. Let me turn to the animals. The fennec fox is my favourite. It is small, with a very short tail, but it has huge ears. Those ears let the heat out of its body, and also help it to hear insects under the sand. And now the people. There are a few groups who live in the Sahara. One of the best-known is the Tuareg. Some people mix them up with the Berber people, who live nearer to the coast, but the Tuareg are the ones who cross the sand with camels. They are often called the blue men. Their clothes are blue, not black, as you may think, because the colour comes from a special dye. The cloth leaves a little of the colour on their skin. If you travel there, be polite, take plenty of water, and listen to the guides. Thank you very much for your attention.

gaps.prompt: Most experts say that the desert crosses ___ countries
gaps.explanation: Some books say nine, but most experts count eleven.

gaps.prompt: Sand covers only about one ___ of the desert
gaps.explanation: A fifth is sand; the rest is rocky mountains and stony plains.

gaps.prompt: In summer the heat in the daytime can reach ___ degrees
gaps.explanation: It can reach fifty degrees; forty-eight was last July’s record.

gaps.prompt: The fennec fox loses heat through its enormous ___
gaps.explanation: The fox has a short tail but huge ears that let the heat out.

gaps.prompt: The people who cross the desert with camels are the ___
gaps.explanation: The Berber people live nearer the coast; the Tuareg cross the sand with camels.

gaps.prompt: The clothes of the Tuareg are ___
gaps.explanation: They are often called the blue men; their clothes are blue, not black.

parts.title: An interview with a desert photographer
parts.instructions: Listen to the interview and choose the correct answer.

turns.speaker: i
turns.text: Adriana, welcome. You are known for your pictures of deserts. Where did it begin?

turns.speaker: p
turns.text: Well, people expect that it started with a trip to Arizona, but I only went there years later. And I wasn’t a big reader as a child, so no book gave me the idea. On my twelfth birthday my father put a camera in my hands. It was old and heavy, but I took it everywhere. He taught me the basics and then left me alone.

turns.speaker: i
turns.text: What do you like about the light in the desert?

turns.speaker: p
turns.text: I love it, and it’s a feeling more than a technique. The sky is not always a bright blue, sometimes it’s white or grey. And the light isn’t the same at noon as at six. What I adore is the way the sand goes from yellow to orange to deep red in a few minutes. You have to be quick, or you miss it.

turns.speaker: i
turns.text: Which part of the work is hardest?

turns.speaker: p
turns.text: It’s the weight. I carry two cameras, long lenses, a tripod, water and food, and in forty degrees every kilo seems like ten. Finding places is not hard, I plan carefully, and the villagers are usually very friendly and happy to talk. But my back is not so happy.

turns.speaker: i
turns.text: Where would you like to go next, and why?

turns.speaker: p
turns.text: The Atacama in Chile. It’s not the cold at night, although it can be freezing, and it’s not for the dunes, they’re not the tallest in the world. I want to go because it’s the driest place on Earth. In some places it hasn’t rained for hundreds of years, and the ground looks like another planet.

turns.speaker: i
turns.text: Is it true that you once waited a long time for a single photograph?

turns.speaker: p
turns.text: Yes, for a lizard. I didn’t travel for a week, it lived near a hotel, and I had my normal lens. I sat very still behind a rock for a whole day, from the morning until dusk. In the end it ran into the light and posed for a second. That was the shot.

turns.speaker: i
turns.text: Tell us about your new book. Why did you choose that subject?

turns.speaker: p
turns.text: It’s not about animals or about the history of photography. It’s about the people who live in the desert. I’ve met so many families who told me their stories over tea, and I felt that I had to share them. A photograph tells you part of a story, but a person tells you the rest.

questions.prompt: What did the photographer get on her twelfth birthday?
questions.explanation: Her trip to Arizona came later and no book gave her the idea; her father gave her a camera on her twelfth birthday.

questions.prompt: How does she feel about the light in the desert?
options: It makes the sky look blue
It changes the colour of the sand fast
It stays the same all day
questions.explanation: The sky is not always blue and the light is not the same all day; the sand goes from yellow to red in minutes.

questions.prompt: What does she find difficult about her work?
options: Carrying heavy equipment in the heat
Finding the right places to go
questions.explanation: Finding places is not hard and the villagers are friendly; the heavy equipment in the heat is the difficult part.

questions.prompt: Why does she want to go to the Atacama?
options: It is very cold at night
It has the tallest sand dunes
It is the driest place on Earth
questions.explanation: It is not the cold or the dunes; she wants to go because it is the driest place on Earth.

questions.prompt: What did she once do for a perfect picture of a lizard?
questions.explanation: She did not travel for a week or use a special lens; she waited behind a rock for a whole day.

questions.prompt: Why did she choose to write about people?
options: They told her stories she wanted to share
She is tired of photographing animals
questions.explanation: It is not about animals or the history of photography; the families told her stories and she felt that she had to share them.
